text: You take about twenty thousand breaths a day. Where does all that air go?
In through your nose or mouth, then down your windpipe, the trachea.
Rings of cartilage, shaped like the letter C, hold it open.
Then it splits into two main bronchi, one for each lung.
The right one is wider, shorter and more vertical.
So in adults, inhaled objects more often land on the right.
Inside each lung, the tubes keep branching, about twenty-three times.
They end in tiny air sacs called alveoli. Hundreds of millions of them.
Here oxygen crosses into tiny blood vessels called capillaries.
Your blood carries it to your heart, which pumps it to your whole body.
Carbon dioxide travels the other way.
Back up the bronchi and trachea, and out with your next breath.
Save this for your next physiology exam.
